en: In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with Annotations, it is said:
"To see all marks as non-marks is to see the Tathāgata. This means that because the dharmas of the Tathāgata are empty, one sees him by being free from marks.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [text fragment].
This passage gives rise to genuine faith that is not the mind of an ordinary person.
Because one takes these causes as signs, fear arises; hearing this principle, there seems to be no place to rest.
The mind... [omitted] ...makes this statement: "The profound essence of Prajñā is for those of the Supreme Vehicle;
it should not be disbelieved that one may awaken immediately upon hearing it."
Do not ask such a question. For those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, they can give rise to faith in these words and phrases;
how much more so now that the True Dharma is circulating?
If one lacks faith, you should know that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one Buddha, two Buddhas,
or even under immeasurable thousands of myriads of Buddhas; they are unable to [master] these chapters and verses.
Even those who give rise to pure faith for a single moment do not see that which can produce [it]; yet they know and see all that has come from the past.
Because these sentient beings have attained [the Buddha-dharma eye],
they are able to see and know all things with complete vision.
These sentient beings of pure faith obtain such immeasurable merit. Why is this?
Because these [beings] do not perceive the mark of a living being (*jīva*) or the mark of a person (*pudgala*).
There is no mark of phenomena, nor is there any non-[mark]. In a single thought-moment, it is pure;
the three emptinesses are suddenly understood.
If one calculates based on various marks,
it cannot be called pure faith;
only then can one truly believe in Prajñā.
One knows and penetrates the emptiness of dharmas;

therefore, one knows that these sentient beings no longer possess any marks. If one were to grasp at the marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, how could one give rise to pure faith? If one grasps at the marks of dharmas...
This is because one would then be attached to the notions of self, person, and sentient being.

If one grasps at the mark of non-dharmas, one is likewise attached to the notions of self, person, and sentient being. One should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at the marks of non-dharmas.
One uses emptiness to destroy existence.
If one becomes stagnant in emptiness and fails to realize non-emptiness, one will again fall into attachment to signs. Thus the Tathāgata has constantly taught.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that I have said this;
how much more so regarding what is not the Dharma? Because one does not grasp at signs, the Tathāgata has constantly taught."
By teaching the non-existence of dharmas, one destroys attachment to existence;
if one knows both existence and non-existence,
one will ultimately awaken to the raft that reaches the other shore.
Because one catches fish by means of a trap but forgets the trap once caught,
and reaches the shore by means of a raft but abandons the raft once there;
such is the view of the Great Sage regarding all views.
Once all views have been eliminated, even the dharma of emptiness is exhausted;
how much more so for that which is not the dharma of emptiness? How could it be otherwise, O Tathāgata?
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [the Buddha] previously caused them to abandon their dharmas and dispelled those two extremes;
thus, regarding the Buddha’s enlightenment...
"How can you alone have attained it and preach the Dharma for others? Subhūti replied, "There is no fixed dharma that can be called 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It is because there is no such thing that the Tathāgata can speak of the unsurpassed right path."
Tranquil and without substance,
one awakens to the signless;
having thus attained bodhi, the Buddha has realized enlightenment.
Upon awakening, there is no Buddha; for this reason,
all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are not to be grasped.
Because sentient beings are devoid of marks,
they cannot be grasped;
because they are beyond words, they cannot be described.
Yet the wondrous is not existent;
it is not non-existent because it is not non-nonexistent. Thus, it is neither existent nor non-existent.

Because it is free from all verbal characteristics... Why is this? It is because although the Buddha should preach the Dharma, there is no fixed dharma to be preached. Why? Because all noble ones and sages...
All [distinctions] exist through the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), yet within the unconditioned dharma there is fundamentally no distinction.

Although the faculties and consciousnesses of the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles differ, when preaching with a single voice, the shallow and the deep follow accordingly; for those who have not yet awakened, one measures their ailments and administers the medicine.
Therefore, he constantly preaches the Dharma;
once awakened, both the medicine and the illness are eliminated, such that there is no dharma to be preached. Subhūti, what do you think?
If a person were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift...
[omitted] ...if a person were to give such a gift of wealth and treasure.
By elucidating the words and phrases,
the merit obtained by this person— whose principle is indeed not false—
is surely great, is it not?
Subhūti said: "It would be very much,
World-Honored One, if the three thousandfold world system were entirely filled with the seven precious jewels."
Why is it that the merit of giving from non-substantiality increases extensively?
It is because this is true merit.
It is not a nature of merit.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great; for because the giving is extensive, the merit is great.
Because it is not of the nature of merit.
If it were of the nature of merit,
then one would not need to treasure [the object] for the merit to be great.
It arises solely from the merit of the absence of intrinsic nature, depending upon external conditions.
For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke of merit. Furthermore, if there should be another person...
In this sutra, to receive and uphold even as little as a four-line verse and explain it for others.
That merit surpasses the merit of that material gift;
it is not of the nature of [mere] merit. Although merit arises because of giving, [it is distinct].
One does not advance toward Bodhi;
yet the merit of upholding this sutra,
though its verses and phrases be few, is [immeasurable].
To enable sentient beings to eliminate the hindrance of afflictions is true merit;
therefore, it is superior to that [other merit]. Why is this so?
Subhūti, all Buddhas and the Dharma of the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas—
From this sutra emerges the correct wisdom of prajñā,
which perfectly illuminates without obstruction—
the unsurpassed right path.
It is because of this that illumination is revealed:
the Buddhas first cultivate themselves and ultimately transform sentient beings.
The benefit and salvation [it brings] are vast and far-reaching; how could it not proceed from this?
That which Subhūti calls the Buddha-dharma is precisely not Buddha-dharma, for dharmas have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
When realized, they are utterly identical.
Because he taught others to realize emptiness, he is called a Buddha.
The Dharma is established through teaching;
realization does not stagnate in emptiness.
To speak directly, there is no dharma that can be negated.
Not only is it the case that even the Buddha-dharma must be negated,
Subhūti, what do you think?
A stream-enterer might think: "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry;
I shall not further cultivate the outflows-free [path], yet I shall realize the outflows-free fruit."
To realize that there is nothing to be attained is called being a *srotāpanna*.
This is by borrowing the "non-self" (*anātman*) of the Hīnayāna.
To clarify that the wisdom of *prajñā* involves the forgetting of signs, Subhūti said:
"No, World-Honored One. Such a person does not give rise to the thought of attaining the fruit. Why is this?
A *srotāpanna* is called one who has entered the stream."
Yet there is no entering;
one does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
This is called the Srotāpanna’s cultivation of the fruit of outflowlessness.
This is called entering the stream of the Path.
Because one does not grasp at the marks of fruition,
there is no stream into which one can enter.
How could one, by forgetting appearances,
lack the flow of the Way to enter? Furthermore,
[how could one do so] while still possessing a self?
Or does he enter into sounds, forms, and the six sense-objects?
Subhūti, what do you think?
Does a Sakṛdāgāmin give rise to such a thought?
When I attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, I did not sever the afflictions of the desire realm through contemplation;
rather, I realized the characteristic of the emptiness of self and phenomena.
At the time of realizing this fruit:
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One.
Such a person does not give rise to the thought of attaining the fruit. Why is this?
Because of the Sakṛdāgāmin."
It is called "once-returning," yet in reality there is no coming or going;
this is called the exhaustion of the destinies of gods and humans for a sakṛdāgāmin.
One attains the fruit of "once-returning.
This "once-returning" clarifies the fruit that has been attained;
one does not grasp at the characteristics of the fruit.
Therefore, in reality, there is no coming or going.
If one perceives a fruit of coming and going,
this gives rise to the conceit of "I."
Then, Subhūti, he would not be a Sakṛdāgāmin.
What do you think? Could an Anāgāmin form such a thought?
When I attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*, I did not sever the afflictions of the desire realm, yet having exhausted them,
I shall no longer return.
This was when I realized the fruit.
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One.
Such a person does not give rise to the thought of attaining the fruit. Why is this?
Anāgāmin is named 'one who does not return.'"
In reality, however, there is no coming;
therefore, he is called an Anāgāmin, one who has realized the non-existence of a person or self and will not return again.
Therefore, it is called the "non-coming" because of the twofold emptiness of person and phenomena;
since there is no characteristic of grasping or abiding,
in reality there is no coming.
That is the Anāgāmin.
Subhūti, since this meaning is thus complete,
what do you think?
An Arhat can have this thought:
"I have attained the path of Arhatship; though I do not cultivate wisdom, I have severed the afflictions."
"At the time of realizing the fruit, does one have this thought? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
Such a person does not give rise to the thought of attaining the fruit. Why is this?"
In truth, there is no dharma called "Arhat" that is designated as an Arhat because of having severed the afflictions.
The nature of afflictions is emptiness;
there is nothing to be severed in severance,
and nothing to be severed in awakening.
"Is there, World-Honored One, yet another Arhat apart from this?
If an Arhat were to form such a thought:"

If I were to think, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," I would then be clinging to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; if I grasp at the characteristics of the fruit,
I am reckoning that there is a self.
If one does not forget the various marks regarding me,
one will invariably cling to marks and receive retribution; all manner of afflictions will arise,
as one takes up marks and undergoes rebirth.
"How could I be called an Arhat, World-Honored One?
The Buddha has declared that I am the foremost among men in attaining the Samādhi of Non-contention;
I am an Arhat who is foremost in being free from desire, and I delight in the practice of solitary retreat."
Having attained samādhi,
he deeply enters into contemplation that is free from conflict and dispute among all people.
It is the most transcendent and supreme;
therefore, it is called "the foremost.
It [overcomes] the afflictions of the three realms.
To be bound by craving for objects as they arise is called desire;
one should completely abandon such things.
Therefore, it is also said that I, the foremost, do not harbor such thoughts:
"I am an Arhat free from desire. At that time, I never once gave rise to the thought: "I am..."
“World-Honored One, there is desire that can be abandoned and there is fruit that can be attained.
If I were to think thus:”
"I have attained the path of Arhatship.
The World-Honored One would not then say, "Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā," were I to give rise to the thought that I have attained a fruit.
Upon attaining the path of freedom from desire,
one immediately becomes attached to a self,
thereby contradicting the practice of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Then, World-Honored One,
you should not say, "I am one who delights in araṇya," for Subhūti,
in reality, there is nothing practiced.
And he is named Subhūti.
He delights in the practice of araṇā; in practice there is no practice.
This is the realization of the characteristic of emptiness. Thus the Buddha addressed Subhūti.
"What do you think?
When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he obtain any dharma? This is to clarify that the Bodhisattva also awakens to emptiness."
Therefore, he asked in return:
"In the past, when I was a bodhisattva,
at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara..."
Regarding the prediction of enlightenment:
at that time, O World-Honored One,
one sees that there is no dharma of enlightenment to be attained.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
he truly attained nothing regarding the dharmas; he realized the emptiness of the nature of phenomena and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
Diligently practice prajñā;
its supreme fruit is called bodhi.
Enter deeply into right contemplation.
The Buddhas grant predictions based on this to Subhūti.
What do you think?
Does a bodhisattva adorn Buddha-fields? Does a bodhisattva cultivate the practices for purifying Buddha-fields?
"Do you see any pure land that can be adorned?
No, World-Honored One. Why is this?"
To adorn the Buddha-lands is itself non-adornment;
it is called adornment because the myriad practices are not eternal.
Ultimately empty and quiescent,
there is nevertheless cultivation;
it is merely designated as "adornment."
The land is fundamentally empty and lacks the characteristics of adornment;
one is able to realize this signlessness.
It is precisely because of this adornment that it is called "adornment. Therefore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
One should give rise to a pure mind in this way:
one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms;
one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. This is because [the mind] is that which is cultivated.
One should not grasp at the signs of adornment;
rather, one should give rise to a mind that is ultimately empty and tranquil in this way.
Because this mind is pure.
Not abiding in form,
nor in sound, fragrance, and so forth;
if regarding these phenomena...
That which arises as a mind is not the fruit realized by a pure mind,
for it is not the ultimate fruit.
It should not be thus; rather, one should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere,
knowing that the characteristics of form are empty,
because the mind dwells nowhere.
Abiding in non-abiding,
one gives rise to a pure mind;
although it is provisionally called "giving rise to the mind," [it is ultimately without self-nature].
Yet there is no characteristic of a dwelling mind;
there is no dwelling in right contemplation,
for the illumination of wisdom is profoundly still.
Subhūti, this is because one abides in the perfection of wisdom by means of the dharma of non-abiding.
For example, it is as if there were a person.
"The body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains.
What do you think?
Is this body great? The characteristic of the body is empty."
For example, although Mount Sumeru has a great name,
it is entirely devoid of substantial reality.
One should not give rise to the thought of grasping at signs,
thereby conceiving of a "great body," which would destroy the previous mind that was grasping at form.
Therefore, Subhūti raised the question regarding the "great body," saying:
"It is exceedingly great, Blessed One.
For what reason?"
The Buddha said that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.
Consider Mount Tai.
Wood and stone share the same altar;
when various materials are combined,
they are conventionally designated as "large."
Since they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature,
how can they be fixed as "great"?
Therefore, the Buddha said they are not bodies.
This is called the "Great Body.
One should not give rise to a mind that grasps at the characteristics of a body.
Subhūti, just as form, sound, and so forth cannot be grasped,
so too are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in such [a number of] Ganges Rivers. What do you think?
Are these grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers [many]?
It would be better to take many rather than one *gaṅgā-vālukā*; that is,
to count the sands within every river.
"It is likewise so.
Is such a number great or not? Subhūti replied:
"Very many, World-Honored One!
Yet even all those Ganges Rivers alone are already countless."
How much more so the sands themselves; even the rivers counted by those sands are incalculable, let alone the sands within them.
They are truly very many, Subhūti.
I now tell you this in truth.
If a son or daughter of good family were to fill as many Ganges Rivers as there are with the seven treasures.
If one were to give as a gift the three thousand great thousandfold world systems,
would the merit obtained be great?
Subhūti said, "It is very much so,
World-Honored One; the merit of that which lacks intrinsic nature is vast,
and the resulting merit is great."
The sands of the Ganges and the great trichiliocosm are immeasurable in number;
thus we know.
The merit thus obtained is exceedingly great. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family..."
In this sutra, even those who merely uphold as few as four lines of verse and explain them to others.
Yet this merit surpasses the former merit; for although material gifts may be numerous,
they do not benefit wisdom and understanding.
Although these chapters and verses are few,
they will surely lead one to Bodhi;
by this comparison, [the merit is established].
Therefore, there is no hierarchy. Furthermore, Subhūti,
wherever this sutra is taught, even so much as a single four-line verse, etc., [there one should know that a stupa of the Tathāgata has been established].
It should be known that in this place, all the worlds—
including devas, humans, and asuras— [are present].
All should be honored;
this is further distinguished as superior to the stupas and temples of the Buddha,
in order to encourage the practice of cultivation.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
if there should be a stūpa, temple, or relic image, and if there is someone who,
in accordance with this sutra, preaches it while also upholding its verses and phrases;
Then gods, humans, and their like should all make offerings [to them],
just as they do to those stūpas and shrines; how much more so for those who possess human form?
Subhūti, you should know that such a person is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
One accomplishes the supreme, foremost, and most rare dharma of the right wisdom of prajñā,
which enables one to proceed toward bodhi.
If a person upholds it, [they shall attain this].
They will certainly give rise to faith and understanding;
one should then know that such a person is capable of accomplishing unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, it is said that this is the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma.
Wherever this sutra may be located, there is a Buddha and there are honored disciples. This refers to wherever the sutra is located.
Thus, there is a person who has achieved the sublime;
since the supreme Dharma resides in that person,
it is as if there were a Buddha.
There was but a slight difference, much like that between a teacher and a respected disciple. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"What should this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it? Regarding what has been clarified previously, there is no fixed dharma whatsoever.
Although the Dharma has no fixed form,
its teaching must have a central tenet.
It is with the desire to proclaim this meaning that [I write].
Therefore, he raised this question. The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should uphold it; it is the wisdom of correct prajñā."
It is like a vajra:
it shatters the hindrance of afflictions and brings one to realize the emergence of the Middle Way.
Because he has crossed the stream of craving and reached the further shore,
he is designated by this name.
This is the immeasurable ultimate truth.
You should examine the name in accordance with its reality and uphold it based upon this. Why is that?
Subhūti, when the Buddha speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
it is not the *prajñāpāramitā*; he speaks of the dharma of *prajñā*.
It remedies the disease of afflictions (*kleśa*). Afflictions are false;
they arise from the grasping of views.
Once delusory illness has been eliminated,
true dharmas should be relinquished;
yet if one clings to the Prajñāpāramitā, [one remains in error].
Because they do not understand the meaning of emptiness,
even this Prajñā becomes a source of affliction.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, regarding the Prajñāpāramitā taught by the Buddha, there is no fixed dharma named 'Prajñā.
What do you think?"
If the Tathāgata has preached any Dharma, that which is not preceded by "not" is not Prajñā;
if one does not yet understand why this is so,
it is not [Prajñā].
Therefore, he sets aside this doubt to clarify the preceding meaning. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One," he said.
The Tathāgata has nothing to say, yet his speech is unhindered;
throughout his life he speaks, yet he never speaks;
regarding all phenomena, he has no grasping.
One may speak for a lifetime and yet never have spoken; as I have taught,
even the Dharma should be relinquished.
Those who are ignorant of this Way speak without understanding; thus,
regarding these two nights...
Subhūti, I have not taught anything at all.
What do you think? As for this trichiliocosm—
"Are all those atoms numerous? Subhūti replied:
"Very much so, World-Honored One. Previously it was explained that the teaching on principles is without grasping.
Subhūti, these objects of illumination are also empty, as are all subtle atoms."
The Tathāgata says that what is not an atom is called an atom;
the Tathāgata speaks of "worlds."
That which is not a world is called a world; having dispersed that world into fine dust,
[one contemplates] within those particles.
They originally lack intrinsic nature;
it is by the accumulation of those subtle atoms that the world is formed.
In this world, how could there be any inherent nature?
Fundamentally, there is no self-nature.
Therefore, it is not composed of atoms;
it is a provisional designation based on conditions.
Subhūti, this is what is called a "world-system."
What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Dharma is fundamentally beyond words;
it is through words that the teaching is established."
The body is fundamentally without marks;
it is because of marks that one perceives the body,
and because of words that teachings are established.
Since one cannot grasp the words to seek the principle,
one perceives the body through its characteristics.
Therefore, one must not perceive the Buddha by grasping at signs. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said that the thirty-two marks are themselves non-marks;
they are merely designated as the "thirty-two marks" as a conventional construct of bodily form.
This serves to represent the Dharma King:
all phenomena are fundamentally empty,
and bodily forms do not exist.
One is able to know that all marks are non-marks;
the marks of form are entirely empty.
Subhūti, this very sublime body is what is called the thirty-two marks.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family...
If one were to give away their body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
and yet another person...
In this sutra, even down to receiving and upholding as little as a four-line verse and so forth.
To explain this to others brings forth even greater merit than the vast amount gained by giving away one's own body and life; yet,
even such superior retribution still remains within the cycle of saṃsāra.

Those who are able to receive and uphold this sutra will have their karmic burdens exhausted and will naturally be free from birth and death; if one were to calculate the measure of such merit, it would be immeasurable.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached,
deeply understood its meaning and intent. This sutra is exceedingly vast.
With tears streaming down his face and weeping in sorrow,
he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!"
"The Buddha has preached such a profound sutra as this.
From the past until now,
the eye of wisdom that I have attained— "
Never before had they heard such a sutra; having previously attained the eye of wisdom,
they perceived emptiness within existence,
and now, upon hearing this sutra, [they realize it further].
Even emptiness is discarded; this is called the Middle Way, for it has never been heard before.
Subhūti understands emptiness and has long attained its profound significance.
Desiring to initiate the teaching in order to manifest it for the sake of future generations,
he wept and wailed in sorrowful lamentation.
He marveled at its rarity, saying, "World-Honored One,
if there should be anyone who hears this sutra..."
When faith is pure, the true mark arises;
one should know that such a person...
To accomplish the most rare and extraordinary merit, to have faith that does not cling to signs—
this is the pure mind; it is the attainment of the pure mind.
One is then able to illumine the true mark of prajñā;
having attained this true mark, one realizes it.
One will certainly proceed toward Bodhi and achieve the fruit of Bodhi;
such a person is then called the World-Honored One of the foremost rare merit.
This is the true mark.
This is the characteristic of being and non-being; therefore, the Tathāgata,
by means of the wisdom of prajñā, speaks of it as the true characteristic (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
One proceeds toward the true mark.
Now, as for the true mark,
how could it possess any marks?
Thus, the wondrous form-dharmakāya is true emptiness without obstruction;
it is not a provisional existence of marks.
"Is it not the case, World-Honored One, that this very characteristic— which is apart from emptiness and signlessness— is not the true characteristic?"
That I have now been able to hear such a sutra as this,
and that I believe, understand, accept, and uphold it,
is not difficult; rather, it is the receiving of a prediction of future enlightenment through personal transmission.
For a long time I have been mistaken regarding the Dharma of emptiness;
now that I hear it explained once more,
it will not be difficult for me to believe and understand it in future lives.
In the final five hundred years,
there will be sentient beings who, upon hearing this sutra, believe,
understand, accept, and uphold it.
Such a person is most rare indeed within the period of the Semblance Dharma;
as the distance from the Sage grows ever greater,
they hear only the Bequeathed Teachings.
He then understands and upholds it;
one should know that such a person has thoroughly realized the profound meaning.
There is none superior to him;
therefore, he is called "the foremost. Why is this?
Because this person is without the mark of a self or the mark of a person.
Why is it that they do not have the mark of a sentient being or the mark of a life-span?
It is because this person is called "foremost among the rare" precisely because they do not cling to such marks as these.
One who is able to believe and understand this sutra shall attain the foremost [state]. Why is this?
Because the mark of a self is itself no-mark.
The mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span—
these are all non-marks; they do not exist within me,
yet one falsely conceives of a self.
Having realized me, one realizes that the mark of the self is not a mark;
thus, one does not cling to a person, a being, a soul, or a life-span. Why is this?
Because one is free from all marks.
Therefore, they are called Buddhas. Why is this?
Because such a person is without self;
thus, they are truly rare.
To be able to be free from all marks is itself bodhi;
therefore, it is rare. Thus the Buddha told Subhūti:
In this way, he confirmed those words; furthermore, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and is not startled,
not terrified, and does not fear it.
You should know that such a person is truly rare, for they perceive distinctions within the unconditioned dharmas.
Thus, the noble and the holy differ in their degrees of excellence. Furthermore,
those of the two vehicles are bound by their attachment to cause and effect.
Those who possess the retribution of merit and virtue,
upon hearing this profound meaning,
will certainly be struck with alarm and fear.
To be able to remain free from fear is already rare;
